module_name: Computer Science & Web Engineering
Web Protocols & Client-Server Architecture
column4: HTTP/HTTPS protocols, RESTful API architecture, browser security, cookies, and CORS.

module_name: Which HTTP status code indicates that a request has succeeded and led to the creation of a new resource on the server?
column4: HTTP 201 Created indicates successful request completion resulting in the creation of one or more new resources.

module_name: 201 Created
column4: Correct. 201 specifically signifies new resource creation.

module_name: 200 OK
column4: 200 indicates standard success, but not specifically resource creation.

module_name: 204 No Content
column4: 204 signifies success with no response body.

module_name: 301 Moved Permanently
column4: 301 is a redirection status code.

module_name: What is the primary function of the Same-Origin Policy (SOP) implemented in web browsers?
column4: SOP prevents a script loaded from one origin from accessing document contents or DOM from another origin without authorization.

module_name: To compress HTTP payloads and optimize network latency
column4: Payload compression is handled by gzip/brotli encoding, not SOP.

module_name: To enforce automatic renewal of TLS/SSL certificates
column4: Certificate renewal is managed at the server/ACME level.

module_name: To synchronize JavaScript variables between client tabs
column4: Tab synchronization uses BroadcastChannel or localStorage events.

module_name: To prevent scripts from one origin from reading private DOM data or responses from another origin
column4: Correct. SOP is a core browser security boundary isolating web origins.

module_name: Which HTTP response header is sent by servers to instruct browsers to permit cross-origin access?
column4: The Access-Control-Allow-Origin response header indicates whether the response can be shared with requesting code from the given origin.

module_name: Strict-Transport-Security
column4: HSTS enforces HTTPS connections.

module_name: X-Frame-Options
column4: X-Frame-Options controls framing to prevent clickjacking.

module_name: Access-Control-Allow-Origin
column4: Correct. This header declares permitted client origins.

module_name: Content-Security-Policy
column4: CSP governs resource loading restrictions to prevent XSS.

module_name: How do HTTP Cookies differ fundamentally from HTML5 localStorage regarding client-server communication?
column4: Cookies are automatically attached to matching HTTP request headers sent to the server, while localStorage remains strictly on the client until JavaScript accesses it.

module_name: Cookies are only accessible over WebSockets, while localStorage works over HTTP
column4: Cookies are native to standard HTTP requests.

module_name: Cookies are automatically transmitted to the server with every matching HTTP request; localStorage stays on the client
column4: Correct. Cookies are sent with HTTP headers; localStorage is never automatically transmitted.

module_name: Cookies store up to 50 MB of data, while localStorage stores only 4 KB
column4: Inverse: Cookies hold ~4KB while localStorage holds ~5-10MB.

module_name: localStorage expires as soon as the browser tab closes, while Cookies never expire
column4: sessionStorage expires on tab close; localStorage persists indefinitely.

module_name: Which of the following HTTP methods are specified as idempotent by the HTTP/1.1 specification (RFC 7231)? (Select all that apply)
column4: An idempotent HTTP method can be executed multiple times without changing the server outcome beyond the initial execution. GET, PUT, and DELETE are idempotent; POST is not.

module_name: GET
column4: GET is both safe and idempotent.

module_name: PUT
column4: PUT replaces state; multiple identical PUTs yield the same server state.

module_name: DELETE
column4: DELETE is idempotent; repeating deletion results in the resource being absent.

module_name: POST
column4: POST creates subordinate resources; repeating POST typically creates multiple distinct records.

module_name: Which of the following HTTP response headers provide defense-in-depth against client-side browser attacks? (Select all that apply)
column4: Content-Security-Policy restricts executable script sources, Strict-Transport-Security enforces HTTPS, and X-Content-Type-Options blocks MIME sniffing.

module_name: Content-Security-Policy
column4: CSP mitigates XSS by restricting allowed script sources.

module_name: Strict-Transport-Security
column4: HSTS enforces encrypted transport and blocks SSL-stripping.

module_name: X-Content-Type-Options
column4: Blocks MIME sniffing attacks by requiring nosniff.

module_name: User-Agent
column4: User-Agent is a client request header identifying the browser software.

module_name: Database Engineering & Relational SQL
column4: Relational database schema design, indexing, transactions, ACID properties, and JOIN operations.

module_name: Which database constraint guarantees that a column contains unique values and cannot store NULL values?
column4: A PRIMARY KEY constraint uniquely identifies each record and enforces uniqueness along with an implicit NOT NULL rule.

module_name: PRIMARY KEY
column4: Correct. Enforces uniqueness and rejects NULL values.

module_name: FOREIGN KEY
column4: FOREIGN KEY enforces referential integrity to another table.

module_name: CHECK
column4: CHECK validates values against a Boolean expression.

module_name: DEFAULT
column4: DEFAULT supplies a fallback value when none is provided.

module_name: Which SQL JOIN type returns all records from the left table and the matched records from the right table, filling non-matching right columns with NULL?
column4: A LEFT OUTER JOIN preserves every row from the left table regardless of whether a matching record exists in the right table.

module_name: INNER JOIN
column4: INNER JOIN only returns rows where keys match in both tables.

module_name: RIGHT JOIN (RIGHT OUTER JOIN)
column4: RIGHT JOIN preserves all right table rows.

module_name: CROSS JOIN
column4: CROSS JOIN produces the Cartesian product of both tables.

module_name: LEFT JOIN (LEFT OUTER JOIN)
column4: Correct. Returns all left table rows plus matched right rows.

module_name: In relational database transactions, what does the "I" in ACID stand for?
column4: ACID stands for Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability. Isolation ensures concurrent transactions do not interfere with each other.

module_name: Indexation
column4: Indexing is a performance mechanism, not an ACID property.

module_name: Idempotence
column4: Idempotence is an API and distributed systems concept.

module_name: Isolation
column4: Correct. Isolation governs transaction concurrency and visibility levels.

module_name: Integrity
column4: Integrity is a general goal, but "I" stands for Isolation.

module_name: Which tree data structure is most commonly utilized by relational database storage engines for table indexing?
column4: B-Tree and B+ Tree structures maintain sorted keys with balanced height, providing logarithmic search, range scan, and insertion performance.

module_name: Splay Tree
column4: Splay trees do not guarantee balanced disk block access.

module_name: B-Tree (and B+ Tree)
column4: Correct. B-Trees minimize disk I/O and support fast equality and range lookups.

module_name: Binary Min-Heap
column4: Heaps are optimized for priority queue extraction (min/max), not search.

module_name: Trie (Prefix Tree)
column4: Tries are used for string autocomplete and dictionary lookups.

module_name: Which of the following SQL statements are categorized under Data Definition Language (DDL)? (Select all that apply)
column4: DDL statements define or alter the structure of database objects (CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE). INSERT and UPDATE are DML.

module_name: CREATE TABLE
column4: DDL command defining schema objects.

module_name: ALTER TABLE
column4: DDL command modifying table structures.

module_name: DROP TABLE
column4: DDL command removing schema objects.

module_name: INSERT INTO
column4: INSERT is a Data Manipulation Language (DML) command.

module_name: Which requirements are necessary for a database table to satisfy Third Normal Form (3NF)? (Select all that apply)
column4: To achieve 3NF, the relation must already satisfy 2NF, and every non-prime attribute must depend directly and non-transitively on the candidate key.

module_name: The table must be in Second Normal Form (2NF)
column4: Normal forms are hierarchical; 3NF requires 2NF compliance.

module_name: There must be no transitive dependencies of non-key attributes on candidate keys
column4: Every non-key attribute must depend directly on the key.

module_name: Every column must contain at least three foreign keys
column4: Foreign keys are not required for normalization tiers.

module_name: The table must never store numeric values
column4: Normalization does not dictate data types.

module_name: Data Structures & Algorithmic Complexity
column4: Asymptotic complexity (Big-O), search and sort algorithms, stacks, queues, and tree structures.

module_name: What is the average time complexity for searching a key in a properly dimensioned Hash Map?
column4: Hash maps compute bucket indices via hash functions, achieving constant O(1) time complexity on average.
Correct. Hash tables offer O(1) average lookup time.

module_name: O(log n)
column4: O(log n) is typical of balanced search trees and binary search.

module_name: O(n)
column4: O(n) represents linear scans and worst-case hash collisions.

module_name: O(n log n)
column4: O(n log n) is standard for comparison-based sorting.

module_name: Which fundamental data structure operates strictly according to the First-In, First-Out (FIFO) discipline?
column4: A Queue enqueues elements at the back and dequeues them from the front, ensuring FIFO ordering.

module_name: Stack
column4: Stacks follow Last-In, First-Out (LIFO).

module_name: Binary Search Tree
column4: BSTs order elements hierarchically by key value.

module_name: Max-Heap
column4: Heaps organize elements based on priority ordering.

module_name: Queue
column4: Correct. Queues adhere to First-In, First-Out.

module_name: What is the worst-case time complexity of the Binary Search algorithm when executed on a sorted array of size n?
column4: Binary search halves the remaining candidate space in each comparison, yielding O(log n) worst-case time complexity.

module_name: O(n)
column4: O(n) is the complexity of linear search.
O(n^2) is characteristic of quadratic algorithms like bubble sort.

module_name: O(log n)
column4: Correct. Logarithmic time complexity.
O(1) is the best-case (finding the element at the midpoint immediately).

module_name: Which comparison sorting algorithm guarantees O(n log n) time complexity in the worst case while maintaining sort stability?
column4: Merge Sort achieves guaranteed O(n log n) worst-case performance by recursively dividing and merging, while preserving relative order for equal elements.

module_name: Selection Sort
column4: Selection sort runs in O(n^2) time.

module_name: Merge Sort
column4: Correct. Merge sort is stable and guarantees O(n log n) in all cases.

module_name: Quick Sort
column4: Quick sort degrades to O(n^2) in the worst case and is unstable in standard form.

module_name: Heap Sort
column4: Heap sort achieves O(n log n) but is not a stable sort.

module_name: Which of the following binary search tree variants automatically rebalance themselves during insertions and deletions? (Select all that apply)
column4: AVL trees and Red-Black trees are self-balancing binary search trees that maintain logarithmic height through tree rotations.

module_name: AVL Tree
column4: AVL trees strictly enforce height balance differences <= 1.

module_name: Red-Black Tree
column4: Red-Black trees use color rules to guarantee balanced depth.

module_name: Unbalanced Binary Search Tree
column4: Standard BSTs can degenerate into linked lists with O(n) height.

module_name: Prefix Trie
column4: Tries are tree structures for string retrieval, not self-balancing BSTs.

module_name: Which algorithms can detect the presence of cycles in a directed graph? (Select all that apply)
column4: Depth-First Search (detecting back-edges using recursion stack states) and Kahn's algorithm (topological sorting using in-degrees) can both detect cycles.

module_name: Depth-First Search (DFS) with node visitation states (White/Gray/Black)
column4: A back-edge encountered during DFS indicates a directed cycle.

module_name: Kahn's Algorithm (Topological Sort with vertex in-degree tracking)
column4: If topological sort cannot process all vertices, a cycle exists.

module_name: Dijkstra's Shortest Path Algorithm
column4: Dijkstra computes single-source shortest paths on weighted graphs.

module_name: Huffman Encoding Tree Generation
column4: Huffman coding creates prefix-free trees for lossless compression.

module_name: Cybersecurity & Network Defense
Network Security & Cryptographic Foundations
column4: Symmetric vs asymmetric encryption, cryptographic hashing, digital certificates, and TLS handshakes.

module_name: What is the essential architectural distinction between symmetric and asymmetric cryptography?
column4: Symmetric encryption employs one shared secret key for encryption and decryption. Asymmetric cryptography utilizes mathematically paired public and private keys.

module_name: Symmetric uses one shared secret key; asymmetric uses a public/private key pair
column4: Correct. Core definition of both cryptographic paradigms.

module_name: Symmetric encryption operates only on hardware tokens; asymmetric is software-only
column4: Both paradigms can run in software or dedicated hardware.

module_name: Symmetric algorithms cannot encrypt binary data
column4: Symmetric ciphers routinely encrypt arbitrary binary streams.

module_name: Asymmetric keys are always 64 bits in length
column4: Asymmetric keys range from 256 bits (ECC) to 4096 bits (RSA).

module_name: Which cryptographic hash function is widely standardized and considered secure against collision vulnerabilities?
column4: SHA-256 (part of the SHA-2 family) remains cryptographically secure against collision attacks. MD5 and SHA-1 have proven collision weaknesses.

module_name: MD5
column4: MD5 has broken collision resistance and must not be used for security.

module_name: SHA-1
column4: SHA-1 has demonstrated practical collision vulnerabilities.

module_name: CRC32
column4: CRC32 is an error-detecting code, not a cryptographic hash.

module_name: SHA-256
column4: Correct. SHA-256 offers 256-bit collision resistance.

module_name: Why is it critical to combine a cryptographic salt with user passwords before hashing?
column4: Salting introduces a unique pseudorandom value per password, preventing attacks using precomputed rainbow tables and ensuring identical passwords produce distinct hashes.

module_name: To allow system administrators to decrypt cleartext passwords for recovery
column4: Hashes are one-way functions; salting does not enable decryption.

module_name: To compress password lengths to fit fixed database column sizes
column4: Cryptographic hashes already produce fixed-length outputs.

module_name: To defend against rainbow table lookups and ensure identical passwords produce unique hashes
column4: Correct. Defeats precomputed dictionary and rainbow table lookups.

module_name: To accelerate server password hashing computations
column4: Salting does not accelerate hashing; key derivation functions are deliberately tuned to be slow.

module_name: During a TLS handshake, what verifies the authentic identity of the remote server to prevent Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) attacks?
column4: The server presents an X.509 digital certificate digitally signed by a trusted Certificate Authority (CA) whose root certificate resides in the client trust store.

module_name: The reverse DNS PTR record of the client router
column4: DNS PTR records are unauthenticated and easily spoofed.

module_name: An X.509 digital certificate issued and signed by a trusted Certificate Authority (CA)
column4: Correct. CA digital signatures validate the server identity and public key.

module_name: The client's local MAC address broadcasted over ARP
column4: MAC addresses only exist on local physical link layers.

module_name: The HTTP session cookie set by a previous request
column4: Session cookies are application-layer artifacts and do not validate TLS endpoints.

module_name: Which of the following algorithms are asymmetric (public-key) cryptographic algorithms? (Select all that apply)
column4: RSA, ECDSA, and Diffie-Hellman are asymmetric algorithms. AES is a symmetric block cipher.

module_name: RSA
column4: Asymmetric encryption and digital signature algorithm.

module_name: ECDSA (Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm)
column4: Asymmetric digital signature algorithm based on elliptic curves.

module_name: Diffie-Hellman Key Exchange
column4: Asymmetric protocol for securely establishing shared keys.

module_name: AES (Advanced Encryption Standard)
column4: AES is a symmetric key block cipher.

module_name: Which password hashing functions feature configurable work factors (computational cost) to thwart specialized GPU/ASIC cracking? (Select all that apply)
column4: bcrypt, Argon2id, and PBKDF2 are deliberately designed password hashing algorithms with configurable memory and CPU cost parameters.

module_name: bcrypt
column4: Features an adaptive cost factor scaling iteration rounds.

module_name: Argon2id
column4: Winner of the Password Hashing Competition; configurable memory and time cost.

module_name: PBKDF2
column4: NIST-approved key derivation function with configurable iteration counts.

module_name: MD5
column4: MD5 is a fast general-purpose hash function unsuitable for passwords.

module_name: Application Security & OWASP Top 10
column4: SQL injection defenses, Cross-Site Scripting (XSS), CSRF mitigation, and least privilege access controls.

module_name: What is the single most effective primary defense against SQL Injection vulnerabilities in application code?
column4: Parameterized queries (prepared statements) ensure user input is treated strictly as data rather than executable SQL syntax.

module_name: Parameterized queries (Prepared Statements) with bound parameters
column4: Correct. Pre-compiles SQL grammar and treats parameters purely as literals.

module_name: Client-side HTML input maxlength attributes
column4: Client-side constraints are trivially bypassed by intercepting proxies.

module_name: Encoding database tables using Base64
column4: Base64 is an encoding, not an encryption or security defense.

module_name: Replacing single quotes with double quotes via regular expressions
column4: Ad-hoc regex blacklists frequently miss evasion bypasses.

module_name: Which attack occurs when an unauthorized action is transmitted from a user that the web application trusts, exploiting ambient credentials like cookies?
column4: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) tricks an authenticated browser into submitting unauthorized requests to a vulnerable application.

module_name: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)
column4: SSRF induces the backend server to make unauthorized requests.

module_name: Buffer Overflow
column4: Buffer overflow is a memory safety vulnerability.

module_name: Directory Traversal
column4: Directory traversal exploits dot-dot-slash paths to access files.

module_name: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)
column4: Correct. CSRF exploits automatic transmission of session credentials.

module_name: What is the principal danger presented by Stored Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerabilities?
column4: Stored XSS persists malicious script into database records, which then executes in the browser of any user who views the infected page.

module_name: Hardware motherboards on client devices suffer permanent physical damage
column4: XSS is a logical browser scripting vulnerability.

module_name: Database indices are automatically wiped after every query
column4: Database integrity is affected by SQL injection, not XSS.

module_name: Malicious scripts execute in the context of victim user sessions, allowing cookie theft and account takeover
column4: Correct. XSS executes attacker JavaScript within the victim's trusted browser session.

module_name: Attacking code can recompile the server-side PHP binary on disk
column4: XSS executes in the client browser, not on the server operating system.

module_name: What is the definition of the "Principle of Least Privilege" in information security architecture?
column4: Every subject (user, process, or system) must be granted only the minimum permissions necessary to complete authorized functions.

module_name: Requiring all servers to run on single-core CPU processors
column4: Hardware specifications are unrelated to privilege management.

module_name: Granting entities only the minimum privileges essential to perform their authorized functions
column4: Correct. Minimizes the potential attack surface and blast radius.

module_name: Granting full root administrator access to all employees to avoid productivity delays
column4: Direct violation of security principles.

module_name: Disabling password requirements on internal local area networks
column4: Weakens access controls.

module_name: Which defensive techniques are effective in mitigating Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerabilities? (Select all that apply)
column4: Context-sensitive output encoding, robust Content Security Policies (CSP), and the HttpOnly flag on sensitive cookies protect against XSS exploitation.

module_name: Context-aware output escaping and HTML encoding before rendering data
column4: Neutralizes executable characters like <, >, and quotes in user content.

module_name: Enforcing a strict Content-Security-Policy (CSP) restricting inline script execution
column4: Prevents unauthorized scripts from executing even if injected.

module_name: Marking session cookies with the HttpOnly attribute
column4: Blocks client-side JavaScript (document.cookie) from reading the session token.

module_name: Disabling all database foreign key constraints
column4: Foreign key constraints have no bearing on XSS mitigation.

module_name: Which security practices defend authentication systems against automated credential stuffing and brute-force attacks? (Select all that apply)
column4: Multi-factor authentication (MFA), progressive rate limiting/delays, and screening against known breached passwords safeguard authentication endpoints.

module_name: Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA / 2FA)
column4: Requires a secondary factor beyond passwords, stopping credential stuffing.

module_name: Rate limiting and progressive login attempt throttling
column4: Limits automated high-volume guess attempts per IP and account.

module_name: Screening passwords against known compromised password databases (HaveIBeenPwned)
column4: Prevents users from choosing passwords already leaked in breaches.

module_name: Logging plaintext passwords into unencrypted server log files
column4: Severe security vulnerability exposing credentials.

module_name: Cloud Infrastructure & DevOps Practices
Containerization & Docker Fundamentals
column4: Container vs VM architecture, Dockerfiles, volumes, networking, and multi-stage image builds.

module_name: What is the architectural distinction between a Docker container and a traditional Virtual Machine (VM)?
column4: Containers share the host operating system kernel and isolate processes using cgroups and namespaces, whereas VMs run a complete guest OS on top of a hypervisor.

module_name: Containers share the host OS kernel; VMs each run a full guest operating system via a hypervisor
column4: Correct. Containers are lightweight process isolations sharing the host kernel.

module_name: Containers require dedicated physical network cards for each running instance
column4: Containers use virtual bridge networks created by Docker daemon.

module_name: Virtual machines can only run on Linux, while containers run on any device
column4: Hypervisors run on all major server operating systems.

module_name: Containers execute exclusively in volatile RAM and cannot write to disk
column4: Containers write to copy-on-write storage layers and persistent volumes.

module_name: In a Dockerfile, what distinguishes the RUN instruction from the CMD instruction?
column4: RUN executes commands during image build time to commit new image layers. CMD defines the default command and arguments executed when a container starts.

module_name: RUN is only executed on Linux hosts; CMD is only executed on Windows hosts
column4: Both instructions are cross-platform Dockerfile standards.

module_name: CMD commits changes to Git; RUN commits changes to Docker Hub
column4: Neither instruction interacts directly with Git or Docker Hub.

module_name: RUN deletes existing layers; CMD restores layers from cache
column4: Neither instruction manages cache restoration in this manner.

module_name: RUN executes at build time to create image layers; CMD defines default container runtime execution
column4: Correct. RUN builds the image; CMD sets the container entry process.

module_name: Which mechanism is recommended for persisting database data across Docker container recreation and restarts?
column4: Docker Volumes and Bind Mounts store data on host filesystems independently of the container lifecycle, ensuring persistence.

module_name: Hardcoding data directly into Dockerfile ENV variables
column4: Environment variables are for configuration, not persistent database storage.

module_name: Rebuilding the image on every database write operation
column4: Impractical and violates immutability principles.

module_name: Docker Named Volumes or Bind Mounts
column4: Correct. Volumes decouple persistent data from container lifetimes.

module_name: The ephemeral container writable layer
column4: The writable layer is destroyed when the container is removed.

module_name: What is the primary operational advantage of multi-stage Docker builds?
column4: Multi-stage builds allow developers to use compilers, SDKs, and intermediate tools in early stages, copying only the final compiled artifacts into a lightweight, secure production image.

module_name: Converting Docker images into virtual floppy disk files
column4: Unrelated legacy storage technology.

module_name: Drastically reducing final production image sizes and attack surface by leaving build tooling behind
column4: Correct. Compilers and headers are omitted from the minimal runtime image.

module_name: Allowing containers to run without an underlying operating system kernel
column4: Containers always rely on the host operating system kernel.

module_name: Enabling containers to bypass network port exposure rules
column4: Network rules remain governed by the container runtime.

module_name: Which Linux kernel mechanisms are foundational to Docker container process isolation and resource limits? (Select all that apply)
column4: Namespaces provide isolated process, network, user, and mount views. Control Groups (cgroups) meter and enforce limits on CPU, memory, and I/O resources.

module_name: Linux Kernel Namespaces (PID, NET, MNT, IPC, UTS, USER)
column4: Provides view isolation for processes, networks, and filesystems.

module_name: Linux Control Groups (cgroups)
column4: Enforces CPU, memory, disk I/O, and resource consumption boundaries.

module_name: Hardware Hypervisor Type-1 firmware
column4: Bare-metal hypervisors (ESXi, Xen) are used for full VMs, not containers.

module_name: Direct BIOS ROM flashing
column4: BIOS flashing is motherboard firmware maintenance.

module_name: Which Docker CLI commands directly manage container lifecycle states? (Select all that apply)
column4: docker run creates and starts a container; docker stop halts execution gracefully; docker rm deletes stopped containers.

module_name: docker run
column4: Creates and starts a container process.

module_name: docker stop
column4: Sends SIGTERM and gracefully halts container processes.

module_name: docker rm
column4: Removes one or more stopped containers from disk.

module_name: docker push-kernel
column4: Not a valid Docker command.

module_name: CI/CD Automation & Version Control (Git)
column4: Git branching strategies, commit history hygiene, automated CI/CD pipelines, and semantic versioning.

module_name: Which Git command creates a new branch and immediately switches your active working tree to it?
column4: git checkout -b <name> (or the modern git switch -c <name>) creates the branch and checks it out in a single step.

module_name: git checkout -b <branch-name> (or git switch -c <branch-name>)
column4: Correct. Combines branch creation and checkout.

module_name: git merge --create <branch-name>
column4: git merge joins branches, it does not create and switch to them.

module_name: git push --new-branch <branch-name>
column4: git push uploads commits to a remote repository.

module_name: git commit --branch <branch-name>
column4: git commit records changes, not branch creation.

module_name: What is the principal difference between `git merge` and `git rebase` when incorporating feature branch commits?
column4: git merge ties branch histories together preserving true commit timestamps and producing a merge commit; git rebase moves the branch base, creating a linear history.

module_name: git merge deletes uncommitted files, while git rebase stashes them permanently
column4: Neither command automatically destroys uncommitted files.

module_name: git rebase can only be used on GitHub servers, not locally
column4: git rebase is a native local Git command.

module_name: git merge converts all commits into binary patches
column4: Git natively stores commits as tree and commit objects.

module_name: git merge preserves exact history with a merge commit; git rebase rewrites commits linearly on the base branch
column4: Correct. Merge keeps branch topology; rebase linearizes commit history.

module_name: What is the primary objective of Continuous Integration (CI) in software development teams?
column4: CI aims to integrate developer working copies into a shared mainline several times a day, accompanied by automated building and testing to catch regressions early.

module_name: Replacing version control repositories with periodic email attachments
column4: CI requires automated source control.

module_name: Automatically deploying untested code directly to customer servers
column4: Deploying untested code violates CI/CD quality gates.

module_name: Frequently merging code into a shared mainline with automated building and testing to surface defects early
column4: Correct. Early automated defect detection is the hallmark of CI.

module_name: Eliminating the requirement for developers to write unit tests
column4: CI relies heavily on developer-written unit tests to validate builds.

module_name: According to Semantic Versioning (SemVer 2.0.0), which version segment MUST be incremented when introducing breaking, backwards-incompatible API changes?
column4: SemVer format is MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. A MAJOR version bump signifies backwards-incompatible breaking API changes.

module_name: BUILD metadata (e.g., 1.4.2+2026)
column4: Build metadata does not denote compatibility semantics.
Correct. MAJOR version changes denote incompatible public API modifications.
MINOR denotes backwards-compatible new functionality.
PATCH denotes backwards-compatible bug fixes.

module_name: Which automated verification steps are standard components of a continuous integration pipeline? (Select all that apply)
column4: Automated unit/integration test suites, static analysis/linters, and security vulnerability scans are standard quality gates in CI.

module_name: Automated unit and integration test suites
column4: Verifies functionality and guards against regression.

module_name: Static code analysis and linter checks
column4: Enforces code style and spots syntax/semantic bugs.

module_name: Dependency security vulnerability scanning (SAST/SCA)
column4: Identifies vulnerable third-party dependencies before merging.

module_name: Physical hardware burn-in testing of developer laptops
column4: Developer laptop burn-in is not part of software CI pipelines.

module_name: Which Git commands rewrite commit history and must be exercised with extreme caution on shared public branches? (Select all that apply)
column4: git rebase, git commit --amend, and git reset --hard alter commit SHAs and history, disrupting peers if performed on shared branches.

module_name: git rebase
column4: Rewrites commit parentage and produces new commit SHAs.

module_name: git commit --amend
column4: Replaces the most recent commit with a revised commit SHA.

module_name: git reset --hard
column4: Moves HEAD and discards commits and working tree modifications.

module_name: git status
column4: Read-only command displaying working tree status.
